cards.front: What do road markings do, and which colors do they use?
cards.back: Road markings guide, warn, and regulate traffic in red, yellow, or white, used alone or combined.

cards.front: Where are red markings used, and which traffic do red reflectors face?
cards.back: Red markings are rare, though some towns use red curbs for no parking; red pavement reflectors face wrong-way traffic only.

cards.front: What do yellow center lines mean, and what does a broken yellow center allow?
cards.back: Yellow center lines mean two-way opposite-direction traffic, and a broken yellow center allows passing on the left in either direction when ahead is clear.

cards.front: With a broken yellow line beside a solid yellow line, who may pass, and when may the solid side cross?
cards.back: A broken yellow line beside a solid yellow line allows passing only from the broken side; solid-side drivers may cross only for pedestrians, bicyclists, or scooter and skateboard riders when the opposite lane is clear and safe.

cards.front: What do double solid yellow lines mean, and when may you cross them?
cards.back: Double solid yellow lines mark the road center between opposing flows: no passing either way, crossing only for left turns or for pedestrians, bicyclists, or scooter and skateboard riders when the opposite lane is clear and safe.

cards.front: How does broken-plus-solid yellow differ from double solid yellow for passing?
cards.back: Broken-plus-solid yellow lets the broken side pass, while double solid yellow lets neither side pass.

cards.front: From the solid yellow side, when may you cross the line?
cards.back: From the solid-yellow side you may cross only for pedestrians, bicyclists, or scooter and skateboard riders with the far lane clear.

cards.front: On an unmarked two-lane road, when may you pass a slow vehicle?
cards.back: On an unmarked two-lane road, you may pass a slow vehicle on the left where no signs prohibit passing and the way is clear.

cards.front: What do broken white lines divide, and what may you do across them?
cards.back: Broken white lines divide same-direction lanes: change lanes with caution.

cards.front: How does a broken yellow line differ from a broken white line?
cards.back: Broken yellow divides opposing directions with passing allowed, while broken white divides same-direction lanes with changes allowed.

cards.front: What jobs do dotted white lines do?
cards.back: Dotted white lines assign lanes through intersections and interchanges, guide paired turning lanes, and mark turn-lane openings and entrance and exit lanes.

cards.front: How do broken white lines differ from dotted white lines?
cards.back: Broken white opens free lane changes, while dotted white steers lanes through intersections and ramps.

cards.front: What do solid white lines mark, and what else uses white markings?
cards.back: Solid white lines mark turn lanes and the right pavement edge, discourage changes near intersections and ramps, and pair with arrows that dictate the allowed turn; stop lines, crosswalks, and parking spaces also use white.

cards.front: What does a yield line of triangles across the road mark?
cards.back: A yield line of triangles across the road, often with a yield sign or at a roundabout entrance, marks where to yield or stop.

cards.front: How do yield triangles differ from white stop lines and parking marks?
cards.back: Yield triangles mark a yield-or-stop point, while white stop lines, crosswalks, and parking marks fix exact positions.

cards.front: What does a curved arrow alone mean compared with a curved plus straight arrow?
cards.back: A curved arrow alone or with ONLY means you must turn that way, while a curved plus straight arrow means you may turn or go straight.

cards.front: How does a curved arrow alone differ from a curved plus straight arrow?
cards.back: A curved arrow alone or with ONLY forces the turn, while a curved plus straight arrow offers turn or straight.

cards.front: What do wrong-way arrows mean, and what should you do?
cards.back: Wrong-way arrows mean you are driving against traffic toward a head-on crash: slow down and pull over at once.

cards.front: What do double solid white lines mean?
cards.back: Double solid white lines divide same-direction lanes, often shielding special-use lanes like HOV lanes: never cross them, entering only where signs and markings allow.

decks.module: Center lanes, bikes and reserved lanes

cards.front: On three-lane two-way roads, what is the marked center lane for?
cards.back: On three-lane two-way roads, the marked center lane serves left turns or passing.

cards.front: What does a center lane with broken yellow on both sides allow?
cards.back: A center lane with a broken yellow line on both sides is open to passing from either direction.

cards.front: What is a center lane with solid plus broken yellow on both sides for, and how far may you travel in it?
cards.back: A center lane with solid plus broken yellow on both sides is open to left turns from either direction, but never to more than one hundred fifty feet of travel.

cards.front: How does a center lane broken on both sides differ from one with solid plus broken lines?
cards.back: A center lane broken on both sides allows passing from either way, while a center lane solid-plus-broken allows only left turns within one hundred fifty feet.

cards.front: What does a sharrow mark, and what should drivers expect?
cards.back: A sharrow pairs a bicycle symbol with a double chevron on lanes too narrow to share side by side: bicyclists ride there and drivers expect them.

cards.front: When may drivers enter a bicycle lane?
cards.back: Bicycle lanes marked by solid or dashed white lines or green pavement with a bike symbol stay preferential for bikes; drivers enter only to turn, after mirror checks and yielding to lane bikes.

cards.front: How does a sharrow differ from a bike lane?
cards.back: A sharrow shares a narrow lane with bikes riding in it, while a bike lane reserves its space with entry only for turns.

cards.front: How must drivers treat a bicycle box at an intersection?
cards.back: Bicycle boxes at intersections hold waiting riders ahead of drivers: stop behind the box on red, never inside it, make no right on red there, and on green signal right turns while yielding to bikes on the right.

cards.front: How are bus-only lanes marked?
cards.back: Bus-only lanes carry BUS ONLY markings, red-colored pavement, or both.

cards.front: How are HOV lanes marked, and who may use them in heavy traffic?
cards.back: HOV lanes carry center diamonds and may run barrier-separated or behind double white lines; in heavy traffic they serve buses, vanpools, carpools, high-occupancy vehicles, motorcycles, and certain clean-fuel vehicles, with signs posting minimum passengers and hours, and barrier lanes reverse direction by time of day.

cards.front: What else can a diamond marking reserve a lane for?
cards.back: A diamond marking can also reserve a lane for buses.

cards.front: How do HOV diamonds differ from bus-only markings?
cards.back: Center diamonds open HOV lanes to qualified high-occupancy travel, while BUS ONLY paint and red pavement close bus lanes to all but buses.

cards.front: What do message boards report, and must you follow them?
cards.back: Portable and permanent message boards report traffic, road, and weather hazards: always obey their directions.

cards.front: How should you drive over rumble strips?
cards.back: Rumble strip warnings mean driving slowly straight over the strips, never swerving around them.

cards.front: How do message boards differ from rumble strips?
cards.back: Message boards issue directions to obey, while rumble strips issue a surface to cross slowly and straight.

cards.front: What vehicles display slow moving vehicle signs, and what should you do?
cards.back: Slow moving vehicles at twenty-five miles per hour or less, such as farm equipment, horse-drawn vehicles, and work vehicles, display warning signs; adjust your speed or position for them.

cards.front: Which payment do all Virginia toll facilities accept, and which lanes do you use?
cards.back: Every Virginia toll facility accepts E-ZPass transponders: follow purple-logo lanes with one, cash lanes without one, slowing with caution for lane changers and crossing employees.

cards.front: What happens if you enter a high-speed E-ZPass lane by mistake?
cards.back: High-speed E-ZPass lanes are transponder-only; a mistaken entry must never stop, since cameras photograph the plate and bill the registered owner.

cards.front: How do purple-logo, cash and high-speed toll lanes differ?
cards.back: Purple-logo lanes serve transponder holders and cash lanes serve the rest, while high-speed transponder lanes punish a mistaken entry with no stopping.

cards.front: What do white, yellow and red painted curbs mean?
cards.back: Painted curbs set parking rules to confirm with the locality: white allows only passenger pickup and dropoff, yellow allows only loading with the driver staying, and red bans stopping, standing, and parking.

cards.front: What do the three painted curb colors each allow?
cards.back: White curbs serve passenger pickup and dropoff, yellow curbs serve loading with the driver present, and red curbs ban stopping, standing, and parking.

recap_hooks.text: Yellow center lines mean two-way traffic; with broken and solid side by side, only the broken side may pass.
Double solid yellow means no passing either way, crossing only for left turns or to give room to pedestrians, bicyclists or scooter and skateboard riders.
Broken white lines allow careful lane changes, while double solid white lines must never be crossed.
A curved arrow alone or with ONLY means you must turn, and wrong-way arrows mean pull over at once.

recaps.module: Center lanes, bikes and reserved lanes

recap_hooks.text: A center lane broken on both sides is for passing, while one with solid plus broken lines is for left turns over a short distance.
Drivers enter a bike lane only to turn, and stop behind a bicycle box on red.
Drive slowly and straight over rumble strips, and always obey message boards.
White curbs are for pickup and dropoff, yellow for loading with the driver staying, and red bans stopping, standing and parking.
